Maudlin

/MAWD-lin/ - the stress falls on MAWD · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Maudlin means weakly and self-indulgently sentimental.

By midnight the campfire talk had turned maudlin, with seniors tearfully vowing to text one another every day forever.

Worked Example

The wedding videographer kept a private folder for toasts that went too far: the best man weeping through a slideshow of childhood haircuts, an uncle sobbing into the microphone about time itself. The couple asked for the short cut.

Maudlin mocks emotion gone soggy — tearful, gushing, and self-indulgent. Genuine feeling isn't maudlin; the word arrives when the tears start performing, and it usually aims at people and their behavior.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

weepy: prone to tears; maudlin adds gushing self-indulgence

gushing: effusively emotional, tears optional

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

composed: feelings held steady and quiet

dry-eyed: unmoved to tears, even when tears were expected

Where it sits · how far the crying tips into excess — sentimental → teary → maudlin

sentimental vs. maudlin: Sentimental is much milder than maudlin — a fondness for old photographs, enjoyed with dry eyes.

teary vs. maudlin: Teary is weaker than maudlin — tears alone can be sincere and brief, while maudlin means the weeping has turned gushing and self-indulgent.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — maudlin

Root — maudlin: from Magdalene — Mary Magdalene, painted forever in tears

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: maudlin is a name worn smooth by centuries of mouths. Mary Magdalene was medieval art's great weeper, always shown in tears; her name — Madeleine in Old French, 'Maudlin' as English said it — slid from the picture to the behavior, and came to mean tearfully, weakly sentimental.

The name hiding inside the word

The name hiding inside the word: Because maudlin is a person's name and not a built word, it has no roots to reuse. Its story is the whole lesson: paint a saint crying for five hundred years, and her name becomes the English word for crying too easily.

Strength Check

Word Choice

critical, mocking

Maudlin mocks emotion that has gone soggy — the tearful toast, the self-pitying reminiscence at midnight. Its unit-mate mawkish aims at the same excess with added disgust, and usually targets works: ads, endings, greeting-card verse. If a person is weeping into the microphone, call it maudlin; if the script made them do it, call the script mawkish.
